thread_title: S. minor var. okefenokeensis Charlton Co, GA
breadcrumb: S. minor var. okefenokeensis Charlton Co, GA

posts.body_html:
After being transplanted and given much more space to grow instead of being packed like sardines, the minor okee giants over a single grow season are already crowding the tubs! They didn't size up, but they certainly put on a lot of growth and a lot of roots, so I think next season on, they'll perform well.

The mother plants were really torn up and abused when they got uprooted last winter, so it takes time for them to recover and build momentum again. Established divisions, on the other hand (eg. once they've been grown for a full season after being divided) have mature root systems, so they can support much larger traps the following grow season.

Pics taken 9/25/22:


they are loving the new peat and are super happy! My daughter Ellie asked how plants can be happy, and I told her to not worry, her daddy ain't koo-koo, it's just a figure of speech:






hard to tell from the pic, but this one has some girth to it:

posts.body_html:
Here's some nice winter colors from November 2022. Some strong yellows and distinct green mouths.


Today, late August 2023, with S. minor var. minor on the right. Not bad, but still under 3' this year.


And a comparison with another S. minor var. okefenokeensis ("Brown Head" ex. Erbacher, I don't know much about this clone but it seems to be common in Europe). I really like the strong upright pitcher habit on the Charlton plant and its reduced ala. "Brown Head" has a lot more areoles and a very strongly recurved domed lid, which I also like. The subtle variations in Okefenokee S. minor are so cool!
